What is Ruby: Ruby is a dynamic, interpreted, reflective, object-oriented programming language created by Yukihiro Matsumoto (Matz) in 1995. It combines syntax inspired by Perl and Smalltalk with object-oriented features. Everything in Ruby is an object — even integers and booleans. Ruby follows the Principle of Least Surprise (POLS), meaning the language behaves as you'd expect. It's known for its elegant syntax, powerful metaprogramming, and the Ruby on Rails web framework.

# Install: ruby --version
# Run: ruby file.rb

puts "Hello from Ruby!"

# Everything is an object
puts 42.class       # Integer
puts true.class     # TrueClass
puts "hi".class     # String
puts nil.class      # NilClass

# Interactive: irb
Ruby Syntax & Conventions: Ruby uses English-like, minimalist syntax. Parentheses are optional for method calls. Blocks defined with do/end or {}. Class and method names follow conventions: SNAKE_CASE for files/variables, CamelCase for classes, snake_case for methods. Files end with .rb. Comments use # for single line and =begin/=end for multi-line. Indentation is 2 spaces (convention, not enforced).

# Naming conventions
file_name = "example.rb"
class UserProfile
end

def calculate_total
  # 2-space indentation
  puts "calculating..."
end

# Optional parentheses
puts "Hello"
puts("Hello")  # same

# Multiline comment
=begin
This is a
multiline comment
=end
Variables & Types: Ruby is dynamically typed. Local variables (name), instance variables (@name), class variables (@@name), global variables ($name), and constants (NAME). Basic types: Integer, Float, String, Symbol, Array, Hash, Boolean, Nil. Type checking occurs at runtime — no static type declarations needed. Symbols (:name) are immutable, lightweight identifiers used for keys and method names.

name = "Alice"       # local variable (string)
@name = "Bob"         # instance variable
@@count = 0           # class variable
$debug = true         # global variable
MAX_SIZE = 100         # constant (warning if reassigned)

# Types
age = 30              # Integer
pi = 3.14             # Float
flag = true           # TrueClass / FalseClass
nothing = nil         # NilClass
sym = :ruby           # Symbol

puts name.class       # String
puts sym.class        # Symbol
Strings & Interpolation: Ruby strings can be single-quoted (no interpolation) or double-quoted (supports interpolation and escape sequences). #{expression} interpolates any Ruby expression. Strings are mutable. Common methods: length, upcase, downcase, capitalize, reverse, split, join, gsub, strip, include?, empty?. << or + for concatenation.

name = "Ruby"
age = 30

# String interpolation (double quotes only)
puts "Hello, #{name}!"       # Hello, Ruby!
puts "Age: #{age}"           # Age: 30
puts "Pi: #{Math::PI.round(2)}"  # Pi: 3.14

# Single quotes = literal
puts 'Hello, #{name}!'       # Hello, #{name}!

# Common methods
puts "hello".upcase         # HELLO
puts "hello".capitalize     # Hello
puts "a,b,c".split(",")    # ["a", "b", "c"]
puts "hello".include?("ll")  # true
Arrays: Arrays are ordered, integer-indexed collections. Can hold mixed types. Index starts at 0. Negative indices count from end (-1 = last). Common methods: push, pop, shift, unshift, first, last, length/ size, include?, empty?, sort, reverse, join, map/collect, select/filter, reject, each, each_with_index. Arrays created with [] or Array.new.

arr = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
puts arr[0]        # 1
puts arr[-1]       # 5
puts arr[1..3].join(", ")  # "2, 3, 4"

# Mixed types
mixed = [1, "two", :three, 4.0]

# Common operations
arr << 6           # append
arr.push(7)        # also append
last = arr.pop     # remove last
first = arr.shift  # remove first

# Iteration
arr.each { |n| puts n }
arr.each_with_index { |n, i| puts "#{i}: #{n}" }

# Transform
squares = arr.map { |n| n ** 2 }
Hashes: Hashes are key-value dictionaries. Keys can be any object type, but symbols are most common (memory efficient, immutable). Two syntaxes: hash-rocket (=>) for any key type, and JSON-style for symbol keys (Ruby 1.9+). Default values can be set. Common methods: keys, values, key?, has_key?, has_value?, fetch, merge, select, each, except, slice.

# Hash with symbol keys (modern syntax)
person = { name: "Alice", age: 30, city: "NYC" }
puts person[:name]     # Alice

# Hash-rocket syntax (any key type)
old = { "name" => "Bob", :key => "value", 1 => "one" }

# Default value
counts = Hash.new(0)   # default 0
counts[:a] += 1        # counts[:a] = 1
puts counts[:b]        # 0 (default)

# Iteration
person.each { |key, val| puts "#{key}: #{val}" }

# Merging
merged = person.merge({ age: 31, country: "US" })

# Selection
adults = { alice: 30, bob: 15, charlie: 25 }.select { |_, age| age >= 18 }
Symbols: Symbols are immutable, reusable identifiers represented as :name. Unlike strings, every instance of a symbol with the same name refers to the same object in memory (same object_id). This makes them ideal for hash keys and method references. Symbols are not garbage collected, so be careful about creating them dynamically from user input. Convert: to_sym / intern, to_s.

:name          # symbol literal
:"with spaces"  # quoted symbol
:"my_var"       # symbol with special chars

# Symbols are singletons
puts "name".object_id == "name".object_id  # false (different strings)
puts :name.object_id == :name.object_id      # true (same symbol)

# Common usage
person = { name: "Alice", age: 30 }

# Conversion
sym = "hello".to_sym   # :hello
str = :hello.to_s      # "hello"

# Method as symbol
objects = [1, "a", 2, "b"]
objects.select(&:to_s)  # shorthand for { |o| o.to_s }

Local & Global Variables: Ruby variables are dynamically typed. Local variables start with a lowercase letter or _, instance variables with @, class variables with @@, and global variables with $. Understanding scope rules prevents subtle bugs. Local vars are scoped to the current block/method; instance vars belong to an object instance; class vars are shared across the hierarchy; globals are visible everywhere (avoid when possible).

name = 'Alice'          # local variable
@count = 0               # instance variable
@@total = 0              # class variable
$debug = true            # global variable

puts defined?(name)      # 'local-variable'
Constants: Constants in Ruby start with a capital letter. They are not truly immutable — Ruby warns but doesn't prevent reassignment. Use them for values that logically shouldn't change.

PI = 3.14159
MAX_USERS = 100

# Ruby warns on reassignment
PI = 3.14  # warning: already initialized constant PI
Data Types: Ruby's core types: Integer, Float, String, Symbol, Array, Hash, true/false (TrueClass/FalseClass), nil (NilClass). Everything is an object — even nil has methods.

puts 42.class          # Integer
puts 3.14.class        # Float
puts 'hello'.class     # String
puts :symbol.class     # Symbol
puts true.class        # TrueClass
puts nil.class         # NilClass

puts 42.to_s           # '42' — Integer#to_s
Type Conversion: Ruby provides explicit conversion methods: to_s, to_i, to_f, to_a, to_sym. Implicit conversion is rare — Ruby prefers raising errors to silent coercion.

age = '25'
puts age.to_i + 5      # 30
puts '3.14'.to_f       # 3.14
puts 42.to_s           # '42'
puts :hello.to_s       # 'hello'

# No implicit conversion
# '5' + 3  # TypeError (String + Integer)

Arithmetic: Standard + - * / % ** operators. Integer division truncates toward zero. ** is exponentiation. Ruby also supports shorthand assignment operators (+=, -=, etc.).

puts 10 / 3   # 3 (integer division)
puts 10 / 3.0 # 3.333...
puts 2 ** 10  # 1024
puts 10 % 3   # 1

x = 5
x += 3        # 8
Comparison: == != < > <= >=. Ruby also has .eql? (type-sensitive comparison) and .equal? (object identity comparison). <=> (spaceship operator) returns -1 if left is less, 0 if equal, 1 if greater.

puts 5 == 5.0   # true (value equality)
puts 5.eql?(5.0) # false (type-sensitive)
puts 5 <=> 10   # -1
puts 10 <=> 10  # 0
puts 10 <=> 5   # 1
Logical: && || ! (and or not). and/or/not have lower precedence than &&/||/!. Short-circuit evaluation applies — && stops on first false, || stops on first true. Ruby uses truthiness (everything except nil and false is truthy).

puts true && false  # false
puts false || 42    # 42
puts !true          # false

# Low-precedence versions (use with caution)
puts true and false  # true (prints true, then evaluates false)
puts (true and false) # false

# Short-circuit
name = nil
display_name = name || "Guest"  # "Guest"
Range: Ruby ranges: inclusive (..) and exclusive (...). Used in iteration, slicing arrays, and case conditions. Ranges can be created from any comparable objects.

range = 1..5
puts range.to_a    # [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

excl = 1...5
puts excl.to_a    # [1, 2, 3, 4]

case score
when 90..100 then 'A'
when 80...90 then 'B'
end

# Range with strings
puts ('a'..'e').to_a  # ["a", "b", "c", "d", "e"]

if/unless/elsif: Ruby uses if, elsif, else, unless, and ternary (?:). unless is the opposite of if and reads naturally for negative conditions. if/unless can be used as statement modifiers (postfix). All conditionals return a value. Only nil and false are falsy — everything else (including 0, empty strings, empty arrays) is truthy.

age = 20

if age >= 18
  puts "Adult"
elsif age >= 13
  puts "Teen"
else
  puts "Child"
end

# unless (opposite of if)
unless age < 18
  puts "Can vote"
end

# Statement modifiers (postfix)
puts "Adult" if age >= 18
puts "Minor" unless age >= 18

# Ternary
type = age >= 18 ? "Adult" : "Minor"

# Truthiness
if 0       # truthy! (unlike some languages)
  puts "zero is truthy"
end

if ""     # also truthy
  puts "empty string is truthy"
end
case/when: Ruby's case/when is more flexible than switch/case in other languages. It uses === (case equality operator) for comparison, which can match classes, regexp, ranges, and procs. when can have multiple values separated by commas. else is the default. Returns the value of the last evaluated expression.

grade = 85

result = case grade
when 90..100 then "A"
when 80...90 then "B"
when 70...80 then "C"
when 60...70 then "D"
else "F"
end

puts result  # B

# === operator matching
case "Hello"
when String then puts "It's a string"
when /^H/ then puts "Starts with H"
end

# Multiple values
case 3
when 1, 3, 5 then puts "Odd single digit"
when 2, 4, 6 then puts "Even single digit"
end
while/until Loops: while executes while condition is truthy. until executes while condition is falsy (opposite of while). Both can be used as statement modifiers. begin/end versions guarantee at least one execution. Loop control: break (exit loop), next (skip iteration), redo (rerun current iteration), retry (restart from beginning).

# while
x = 0
while x < 5
  puts x
  x += 1
end

# until
y = 0
until y == 5
  puts y
  y += 1
end

# Statement modifiers
i = 0
puts i += 1 while i < 5

# begin/end (do at least once)
z = 10
begin
  puts z
  z += 1
end while z < 5  # runs once

# Loop control
[1, 2, 3, 4, 5].each do |n|
  next if n.even?  # skip evens
  break if n > 4    # stop at 5
  puts n
end
for/in & each: Ruby has for/in loops but they're rarely used — each and friends are preferred. for/in iterates over enumerables but doesn't create a new scope for the variable (leaks it). each and the Enumerable module provide a rich set of iteration methods with proper scoping. Range literals (1..10) are commonly used for iteration.

# for loop (rarely idiomatic)
for i in 1..5
  puts i
end
puts i  # i leaks! (5)

# each (idiomatic)
(1..5).each { |i| puts i }

# each with index
%w[a b c].each_with_index { |v, i| puts "#{i}: #{v}" }

# Times, upto, downto, step
3.times { puts "hi" }
1.upto(5) { |n| puts n }
5.downto(1) { |n| puts n }
0.step(10, 2) { |n| puts n }  # 0, 2, 4, ..., 10

# Ranges
(1..5).to_a    # [1,2,3,4,5] (inclusive)
(1...5).to_a   # [1,2,3,4] (exclusive)

Defining Methods: Methods defined with def/end. Parentheses optional. Return last evaluated expression implicitly or use explicit return. Method names can end with ? (predicates, return boolean), ! (dangerous/mutating version), = (setter). Arguments can have default values. Keyword arguments (Ruby 2.0+) for named parameters. Splat (*) captures multiple args. Double splat (**) captures keyword args.

# Implicit return (last expression)
def add(a, b)
  a + b
end

# Explicit return
def max(a, b)
  return a if a > b
  b
end

# Default arguments
def greet(name = "World")
  "Hello, #{name}!"
end

# Keyword arguments
def configure(host:, port: 3000, debug: false)
  puts "#{host}:#{port} (debug=#{debug})"
end

configure(host: "localhost")  # localhost:3000
configure(host: "app", port: 8080, debug: true)

# Splat

def sum(*numbers)
  numbers.sum
end

puts sum(1, 2, 3, 4)  # 10

# Predicate methods (end with ?)
puts [].empty?        # true
puts 5.odd?           # true

# Bang methods (end with !)
name = "ruby"
name.upcase!          # modifies in place
puts name             # RUBY
Procs & Lambdas: Procs and lambdas are closures — blocks of code that capture their surrounding environment. Blocks (do/end or {}) are syntactic structures that become Procs when captured with &. Lambda checks argument count (strict), Proc doesn't. Lambda returns from itself, Proc returns from the enclosing method. Use lambdas for strict argument checking.

# Block (implicit)
[1, 2, 3].each { |n| puts n }

# Block to proc with &
def run_block(&block)
  block.call
end
run_block { puts "Hello" }

# Proc
p = Proc.new { |x| x * 2 }
puts p.call(5)  # 10
puts p[5]       # 10 (shorthand)

# Lambda
l = ->(x) { x * 2 }
puts l.call(5)  # 10

# Difference: argument checking
p = Proc.new { |a, b| [a, b] }
puts p.call(1).inspect     # [1, nil] (fills missing with nil)
puts p.call(1, 2, 3).inspect  # [1, 2] (ignores extra)

l = ->(a, b) { [a, b] }
# l.call(1)  # ArgumentError (wrong number)
# l.call(1, 2, 3)  # ArgumentError

# Difference: return behavior
def test_proc
  p = Proc.new { return "from proc" }
  p.call
  "from method"
end
def test_lambda
  l = -> { return "from lambda" }
  l.call
  "from method"
end
puts test_proc    # "from proc"
puts test_lambda  # "from method"
Splat & Keyword Arguments: Ruby methods support flexible argument patterns. Splat (*) captures multiple positional arguments into an array. Double splat (**) captures keyword arguments into a hash. Keyword arguments (Ruby 2.0+) provide named parameters with optional defaults. Arguments can have default values. The order is: positional, optional, splat, keyword, double splat, block (&).
Method Visibility (public/private/protec: Ruby methods have three visibility levels. public — called by anyone (default). private — only callable without a receiver (self implicit). protected — callable within the same class hierarchy, even from different instances. private and protected are declared with `private`/`protected` keywords or by listing method names as symbols after the keyword. Unlike some languages, Ruby's private is more like "internal".

class Person
  def initialize(name, age)
    @name = name
    @age = age
  end

  # Public by default
  def introduce
    "Hi, I'm #{@name}"
  end

  # Protected — can be called by other instances of same class
  def age
    @age
  end

  def older_than?(other)
    age > other.age  # protected allows cross-instance call
  end

private

  def secret
    "shh!"
  end
  # Or: private :secret

protected :age
end
Method Aliases & Undef: alias creates a copy of a method under a new name. alias_method does the same (preferred in modules). undef removes a method (prevents inheritance). Useful for method decoration, AOP, and library design.

class Greeter
  def hello
    "Hello!"
  end
  alias hi hello  # hi is now an alias for hello

  def greet(name)
    "Hello, #{name}!"
  end
  alias_method :greeting, :greet
end

g = Greeter.new
puts g.hello  # "Hello!"
puts g.hi     # "Hello!" (same method)

# undef — removes method
class SilentGreeter < Greeter
  undef hello  # removes hello method
  undef_method :greet  # removes greet method
end

Classes & Objects: Ruby is pure object-oriented. Classes defined with class/end. Constructor is initialize. Instance variables (@name) are private by default. attr_reader, attr_writer, attr_accessor create getters/setters automatically. self refers to the current object. Class methods defined with self.method_name. Every class inherits from Object (which inherits from BasicObject).

class Person
  # Attribute shortcuts
  attr_reader :name     # getter only
  attr_accessor :age    # getter + setter

  # Constructor
  def initialize(name, age = 0)
    @name = name
    @age = age
  end

  # Instance method
  def introduce
    "Hi, I'm #{@name}, age #{@age}"
  end

  # Class method
  def self.species
    "Homo sapiens"
  end

  # Custom setter
  def name=(value)
    raise "Invalid name" if value.nil? || value.empty?
    @name = value
  end
end

# Usage
alice = Person.new("Alice", 30)
puts alice.introduce       # Hi, I'm Alice, age 30
puts alice.name            # Alice (via attr_reader)
alice.age = 31             # (via attr_accessor)
puts Person.species        # Homo sapiens
Inheritance: Ruby supports single inheritance with the < operator. Modules provide multiple inheritance-like behavior via mixins. super calls the parent method with the same arguments. Method resolution order (MRO) follows the lookup path: object -> class -> modules (reverse order of include) -> superclass. ancestor chain shows inheritance.

class Animal
  def speak
    "#{@name} makes a sound"
  end

  def initialize(name)
    @name = name
  end
end

class Dog < Animal
  def speak
    "#{@name} barks!"
  end

  def wag_tail
    "#{@name} wags tail"
  end
end

class Cat < Animal
  def speak
    "#{@name} meows"
  end
end

dog = Dog.new("Rex")
cat = Cat.new("Whiskers")
puts dog.speak   # Rex barks!
puts cat.speak   # Whiskers meows
puts dog.wag_tail  # Rex wags tail

# Ancestor chain
puts Dog.ancestors.inspect
# Dog, Animal, Object, Kernel, BasicObject
Modules & Mixins: Modules collect methods and constants. They cannot be instantiated. Use include for instance methods (mixins), extend for class methods, and prepend to override methods (prepended module methods are called first). Namespacing: MyModule::MyClass. The include lookup checks modules in reverse order of inclusion. Enumerable and Comparable are built-in mixin examples.

module Greetable
  def greet
    "Hello, I'm #{@name}"
  end
end

module Walkable
  def walk
    "#{@name} is walking"
  end
end

class Robot
  include Greetable
  include Walkable

  def initialize(name)
    @name = name
  end
end

robot = Robot.new("R2D2")
puts robot.greet  # Hello, I'm R2D2
puts robot.walk   # R2D2 is walking

# extend (class methods)
module ClassMethods
  def version
    "1.0"
  end
end

class App
  extend ClassMethods
end

puts App.version  # 1.0

# Namespacing
module Admin
  class User
    def role = "admin"
  end
end

user = Admin::User.new
puts user.role

Enumerable Module: Enumerable is Ruby's most powerful mixin. Include it + define each and you get map, select, reject, reduce, any?, all?, none?, one?, count, group_by, partition, sort_by, first, take, drop, min, max, min_by, max_by, each_slice, each_cons, cycle, detect/find, grep, flat_map, zip, chunk, and many more. Lazy enumerators (lazy) for infinite sequences.

numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

# Map / Collect
squares = numbers.map { |n| n ** 2 }

# Select / Find all
evens = numbers.select(&:even?)  # [2, 4]

# Reject
odds = numbers.reject(&:even?)   # [1, 3, 5]

# Reduce / Inject
sum = numbers.reduce(0) { |acc, n| acc + n }  # 15
# Or shorter:
sum = numbers.reduce(:+)  # 15

# Any? / All? / None?
puts numbers.any?(&:even?)   # true
puts numbers.all? { |n| n > 0 }  # true

# Group by
by_parity = numbers.group_by(&:even?)
# { false => [1,3,5], true => [2,4] }

# Each slice
numbers.each_slice(2) { |slice| puts slice.inspect }
# [1, 2]
# [3, 4]
# [5]

# Lazy enumeration
infinite = (1..Float::INFINITY).lazy
  .select(&:even?)
  .first(5)
# [2, 4, 6, 8, 10]
Arrays Deep: Beyond basic array operations, Ruby provides powerful methods: combination, permutation, product, zip, transpose, flatten, uniq, difference (&), union (|), sample, shuffle, rotate, cycle, bsearch, pack. Many accept blocks for advanced transformations.

arr = [1, 2, 3]

# Combinations & permutations
arr.combination(2).to_a  # [[1,2], [1,3], [2,3]]
arr.permutation(2).to_a  # [[1,2], [1,3], [2,1], [2,3], [3,1], [3,2]]
arr.product([4, 5])      # [[1,4], [1,5], [2,4], [2,5], [3,4], [3,5]]

# Zip
a = [1, 2]; b = ['a', 'b']
a.zip(b)  # [[1, "a"], [2, "b"]]

# Set-like operations
[1, 2, 3] & [2, 3, 4]  # [2, 3] (intersection)
[1, 2, 3] | [3, 4, 5]  # [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] (union)
[1, 2, 3] - [2]         # [1, 3] (difference)

# Sampling & shuffling
[1, 2, 3, 4, 5].sample(2)  # random selection
[1, 2, 3].shuffle           # random order

# Binary search (sorted arrays)
[1, 3, 5, 7, 9].bsearch { |x| x >= 5 }  # 5
Hashes Deep: Hashes support advanced features: default procs (compute defaults dynamically), fetch with block (safe access), transform_keys/transform_values (bulk conversion), slice/except (subselection), dig (nested access), compact (remove nil values). The merge method accepts a block for conflict resolution.
Sets: Set implements a collection of unique values. It requires `require 'set'`. Sets provide mathematical set operations: union (+ or |), intersection (&), difference (-), subset?/superset?/disjoint? Also: add, delete, include?, each, map (returns array). Sets ensure uniqueness unlike arrays.

require 'set'

set1 = Set.new([1, 2, 3])
set2 = Set.new([3, 4, 5])

# Set operations
puts set1 | set2   # #<Set: {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}>  (union)
puts set1 & set2   # #<Set: {3}>              (intersection)
puts set1 - set2   # #<Set: {1, 2}>           (difference)

# Comparison
set1.subset?(set2)   # false
Set[1, 2].subset?(set1)  # true
set1.disjoint?(set2) # false

# Auto-deduplication
Set.new([1, 1, 2, 2, 3])  # #<Set: {1, 2, 3}>
Enumerable Chaining & Lazy: Enumerable methods can be chained for expressive data pipelines. Each method returns a new Enumerable. Lazy enumeration (Enumerator::Lazy) defers computation until needed — useful for large or infinite collections. Use .lazy to create a lazy enumerator, then force evaluation with .to_a, .first, or .each.

# Method chaining
[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
  .select(&:odd?)
  .map { |n| n ** 2 }
  .reject { |n| n < 10 }
  .each { |n| puts n }

# Lazy enumeration — processes on demand
big_data = (1..Float::INFINITY).lazy
  .select(&:even?)
  .map { |n| n * n }
  .first(5)
puts big_data.inspect  # [4, 16, 36, 64, 100]

# Lazy file processing
lines = File.foreach("big_file.txt").lazy
  .map(&:chomp)
  .reject(&:empty?)
  .first(100)

# Each with index (returns enumerator if no block)
%w[a b c].each_with_index.map { |v, i| "#{i}: #{v}" }
Enumerator & Generators: Enumerator wraps iteration as an object. Create with Enumerator.new or from methods like each. External iteration with next/rewind/peek/feed. Enumerators can be infinite. Fiber-based generators provide coroutine-like behavior.

# Custom enumerator
gen = Enumerator.new do |y|
  y << 1
  y << 2
  y << 3
end
puts gen.next  # 1
puts gen.next  # 2
puts gen.peek  # 3 (next without consuming)
puts gen.next  # 3

# Infinite enumerator
fib = Enumerator.new do |y|
  a = b = 1
  loop do
    y << a
    a, b = b, a + b
  end
end
puts fib.first(8).inspect  # [1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21]

# Rewind
gen.rewind
puts gen.next  # 1 again

# From existing method
enum = [1, 2, 3].each  # Enumerator
puts enum.with_index.map { |n, i| n * i }

begin/rescue/ensure: Ruby uses begin/rescue/ensure/else for exception handling. rescue catches exceptions by class. Multiple rescue blocks for different exceptions. ensure always runs (like finally). else runs if no exception. raise/throw to trigger errors. $! contains last exception, $@ contains backtrace. StandardError is the common superclass (most code should rescue StandardError, not Exception).

def divide(a, b)
  begin
    result = a / b
  rescue ZeroDivisionError => e
    puts "Error: #{e.message}"
    nil
  rescue TypeError => e
    puts "Type error: #{e.message}"
    nil
  else
    puts "No error occurred"
    result
  ensure
    puts "This always runs"
  end
end

puts divide(10, 2)  # No error occurred / This always runs / 5
puts divide(10, 0)  # Error: divided by 0 / This always runs / nil

# Inline rescue (risky, catches all StandardError)
value = risky_call() rescue "default"

# Custom exceptions
class MyError < StandardError; end
raise MyError, "Something went wrong"

Reading & Writing Files: File operations with File class. Block form auto-closes. Modes: r (read), w (write, truncate), a (append), r+ (read/write), w+ (read/write, truncate), a+ (read/append). Binary mode: rb, wb. Common methods: File.read, File.write, File.readlines, File.foreach (memory efficient for large files). Dir for directory operations. Pathname for path manipulation.

# Block form (auto-closes)
File.open("example.txt", "w") do |f|
  f.puts "Line 1"
  f.puts "Line 2"
end

# Simple read/write
content = File.read("example.txt")
puts content

# Read lines into array
lines = File.readlines("example.txt")
puts lines.length

# Memory-efficient line-by-line
File.foreach("example.txt") do |line|
  puts line.chomp  # chomp removes trailing newline
end

# Append
File.write("log.txt", "New entry\n", mode: "a")

# Check existence
puts File.exist?("example.txt")  # true

# Directory operations
Dir.mkdir("mydir") unless Dir.exist?("mydir")
Dir.entries(".").each { |entry| puts entry }

RubyGems & Bundler: RubyGems is the package manager for Ruby libraries (gems). Bundler manages gem dependencies via Gemfile. Key commands: gem install, gem list, bundle init, bundle install, bundle exec. Gemfile specifies sources and gems. Gemfile.lock locks versions. gemspec for gem development. Popular gems: rails, sinatra, rspec, devise, sidekiq, nokogiri, httparty.

# Install gems
gem install sinatra
gem install rspec

# Gemfile
# source "https://rubygems.org"
# gem "sinatra"
# gem "rspec", group: :test
# gem "puma"

# Bundle commands
# bundle init       # Create Gemfile
# bundle install    # Install gems
# bundle exec ruby app.rb  # Run with locked gems

# Using gems in code
require "sinatra"

get "/" do
  "Hello from Sinatra!"
end

Minitest & RSpec: Ruby's standard testing library is Minitest (built-in, no install needed). RSpec is the most popular third-party testing framework (BDD-style). Minitest uses assert methods. RSpec uses describe/it/expect syntax. Both support before/after hooks, let helpers, and matchers. Test-driven development is common in the Ruby community.

# Minitest (built-in)
require "minitest/autorun"

class TestCalculator < Minitest::Test
  def setup
    @calc = Calculator.new
  end

  def test_add
    assert_equal 5, @calc.add(2, 3)
  end

  def test_subtract
    assert_equal 1, @calc.subtract(3, 2)
  end
end
